sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Creative and scientific image collections embody substantial human labor, expertise, and investment. Adapting text-to-image (T2I) models to such collections can support legitimate personalization, education, design, and scientific communication [ 26 , 7 , 11 ] . The same capability, however, allows a third party to fine-tune and deploy a model on a collection without the rights holder’s consent, attribution, or compensation. Because a model can absorb a collection’s visual characteristics without reproducing individual images, rights holders may have little evidence that their work was used [ 21 , 13 ] . Practical dataset-use auditing can strengthen accountability and licensing compliance while allowing images to remain available for legitimate use. Figure 1 : SpectralCanary overview. (a) Auditing workflow. An owner protects a collection before release, then queries a suspect T2I model and tests whether its generated outputs contain the canary. (b) Spectral hybridization. SpectralCanary blends a fixed canary through a smooth low-pass mask M c M_{c} with strength α \alpha , retaining most of the remaining spectrum. A lightweight verifier trained on original–protected pairs detects the trace in model generations. (c) Visual fidelity. Original–protected pairs across five datasets, including sparse sketches. We study proactive dataset-use auditing, commonly termed data traceability or unauthorized data-use verification in prior works. A practical method should satisfy four requirements. (Req. 1) Collection-level verifiability. It should provide evidence from black-box outputs even when no training image is reproduced. (Req. 2) Fidelity and utility preservation. Protected samples should preserve their original appearance and the utility of models trained on them, avoiding harm to legitimate use while resisting easy filtering. (Req. 3) Pipeline robustness. The trace should remain detectable across model architectures, after augmentation such as image regeneration or recaptioning. (Req. 4) Operational deployability. The protection transform should be model-agnostic and scale efficiently to large collections without auxiliary generation or iterative per-image optimization. Prior approaches typically sacrifice at least one requirement. Reactive auditing: limited collection-level evidence (Req. 1). Membership and similarity tests rely on sample-specific evidence that generalization may erase [ 21 , 13 ] . Pixel-level watermarks: limited robustness (Req. 3). Weak signals may be attenuated by augmentation, regeneration, or fail to transfer across model backbones [ 34 , 13 ] . Explicit canaries: fidelity and robustness trade-offs (Reqs. 2–3). Repeated templates can be conspicuous and filterable, while recaptioning can remove textual triggers [ 25 ] . Adjacent data-poisoning objectives. Poisoning induces chosen behavior rather than provides evidence of dataset use. Persistent behavior may not be unique or reliably elicited, so it does not by itself establish use of a particular collection [ 33 , 12 ] . Across proactive methods, auxiliary generation, filtering, and iterative optimization can also limit deployability (Req. 4) by increasing computational cost or requiring external models, domain-specific assumptions [ 25 , 13 , 12 ] . These limitations motivate a subtle, transferable, caption-independent, and inexpensive trace. We propose SpectralCanary , whose key design choice is the frequency band used for the shared trace. Before release, the dataset owner chooses one fixed canary image. For each collection image, SpectralCanary mixes a small amount of the canary’s low-frequency Fourier content into the original while retaining most of its spectrum and leaving its caption unchanged (Fig. 1 (b)). The protected spectra are thereby shifted toward a common low-frequency target, creating a collection-level signal. Low frequencies encode broad spatial structure that neural networks preferentially learn [ 24 , 37 ] and that is important to T2I generation [ 39 , 17 ] . This motivates our hypothesis that a weak low-frequency trace can transfer during fine-tuning. The dataset owner then queries a suspect model and uses a lightweight verifier to test whether its generated outputs contain the trace (Fig. 1 (a)). Importantly, SpectralCanary uses a single deterministic transform requiring no caption changes, auxiliary generator, or per-image optimization. We evaluate all four requirements. Robustness tests cover a convolutional latent-diffusion U-Net [ 26 ] , a transformer-based rectified-flow model [ 7 ] ; data augmentation, image regeneration [ 42 ] , and recaptioning. Direct baselines include pixel-level traces (SIREN [ 13 ] , DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] ) and explicit canaries (EnTruth [ 25 ] ). We also adapt Silent Branding [ 12 ] but report its evaluation separately in Appx. Q , because it targets visual branding rather than dataset-use auditing. Auditing effectiveness and robustness. For per-generation discrimination, AUC measures verifier-score separation, while TPR at 1% FPR measures detection of outputs from protected-data models. Across eight Pokemon settings, SpectralCanary achieves 98.0% AUC and 91.1% TPR. In fixed-threshold model-level verification using 30 generations, it achieves 94.8% average accuracy under the same settings. Fidelity and utility preservation. SSIM and LPIPS compare original and protected images, while Δ \Delta FID measures the change in generative quality. Across five visual domains with SD3.5, SpectralCanary achieves 99.5 % 99.5\% AUC and 92.4 % 92.4\% TPR with SSIM 0.989 0.989 , LPIPS 0.022 0.022 , with a near-zero mean change FID ( Δ \Delta FID 0.05 0.05 ). On sparse Sketch-Scene drawings, it achieves 100 % 100\% AUC and TPR with SSIM 0.997 0.997 and LPIPS 0.002 0.002 . Operational deployability. Protection takes 0.39 0.39 seconds per image on our CPU setup (Appx. E ). Mechanism and boundary. In matched-energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2, we show that low-frequency placement transfers more reliably compared to mid/high-frequency placement. Within the evaluated adaptive attacks, effective removal requires aggressive modification and incurs more than 25 25 Δ \Delta FID points. Our main contributions are: • We identify low-frequency visual structure as an effective carrier for weak collection-level traces during T2I fine-tuning. In matched band size and perturbation energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2 with SD1.5, we show that low-frequency placement yields higher per-generation TPR than mid/high-frequency placement. • We introduce SpectralCanary, a deterministic and caption-preserving spectral hybridization method. It protects each image with one inexpensive transform, requiring neither an auxiliary generator nor per-image optimization. • We jointly evaluate per-generation discrimination, KS-based multi-query auditing, fixed-threshold model-level verification, image fidelity, generative utility, robustness, and protection cost across two architecture families, five datasets, three direct auditing baselines, an adapted poisoning baseline, and three realistic data transformations. This evaluation establishes a strong empirical operating point and characterizes the boundary under adaptive spectral replacement.

sections.heading: 3 Related Work
sections.text: Reactive and proactive auditing. Reactive methods test an already trained model using membership inference or similarity between generated and reference images [ 3 , 21 , 23 , 19 ] . Such evidence can weaken when fine-tuning transfers collection-level characteristics without retaining identifiable information about individual samples. Proactive methods instead modify a collection before release. Anti-learning methods aim to prevent or redirect customization [ 30 , 43 , 32 , 1 , 15 ] . Proactive traceability aims to preserve customization utility while making later use statistically auditable. Proactive traceability. Pixel-level methods such as DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] and SIREN [ 13 ] insert weak transformations or learned signals that can be detected in generated images. Their subtle signals preserve appearance, but can be attenuated by augmentation, regeneration, or model backbone changes. EnTruth instead inserts explicit canary samples containing a repeated template and textual trigger [ 25 ] . This coherent signal can transfer strongly, but the injected samples are conspicuous and caption triggers can be removed. Our direct comparisons span the two main proactive families including subtle pixel-level traces and explicit visual canary samples. Relation to poisoning. Data poisoning induces chosen behaviors such as concept corruption, reproduction, or persistent branding [ 33 , 12 ] . Persistence alone is insufficient for auditing. Auditing instead requires a collection-specific signal detectable under ordinary, trigger-free queries with controlled false positives. SpectralCanary targets this auditing objective rather than model corruption. Appx. S provides further discussion and a method taxonomy.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup and How to Read the Results
sections.text: Our experiments ask four concrete questions. First, can SpectralCanary reveal that a model was trained on a protected collection, even when the model architecture or training data are changed? Second, does adding the trace visibly change the released images or make a model trained on them produce worse images? Third, is protection fast enough for a large collection? Finally, why do low frequencies matter, and what happens when an informed attacker tries to remove the trace? Datasets and models. We cover distinct image domains: charater art (Pokemon-BLIP-Captions [ 22 ] ), sparse scene drawings (Sketch-Scene [ 4 ] ), medical (ROCOv2 [ 27 ] ), satellite (RSICD [ 16 ] ), and fashion (FACAD [ 38 ] ). We fine-tune Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD1.5) [ 26 ] and Stable Diffusion 3.5 (SD3.5) [ 7 ] . The main experiments use LoRA, a common parameter-efficient form of T2I adaptation. Appx. G repeats the key test with full-parameter fine-tuning. Comparisons and stress tests. We compare with SIREN [ 13 ] and DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] , which modify training images, and EnTruth [ 25 ] , which adds explicit canary samples. Appx. Q separately adapts Silent Branding [ 12 ] , whose original goal is visual branding rather than dataset-use auditing. On Pokemon, we test each method under ordinary training and after three realistic changes to the training set: image augmentation, diffusion-based recreation of each training image (image regeneration) [ 42 ] , and automatic recaptioning with Qwen2.5-VL 7B [ 2 ] . How to read the metrics. We distinguish the embedded trace from two evaluation levels. Per-generation discrimination scores each generated image independently and asks whether outputs from protected-data models receive higher verifier scores than outputs from clean-data models. AUC summarizes this score separation over all thresholds. TPR at 1 % 1\% FPR is the fraction of outputs from protected-data models detected at a threshold that falsely flags at most 1 % 1\% of outputs from clean-data models; thus, a TPR of 90 % 90\% means detecting about 90 of 100 protected-data-model outputs while flagging about 1 of 100 clean-data-model outputs. At the model level, we evaluate two decision protocols. KS-based multi-query auditing combines scores from 30 generated images in a statistical test and reports the rejection rate on protected-data models. Fixed-threshold model-level verification aggregates 30 generations from each held-out model and applies a threshold fixed after independent calibration, reporting TPR, FPR, precision, F1, and accuracy (Appx. H ). For image fidelity, lower LPIPS [ 41 ] means that a protected image is closer to its original. For generated-image quality, Δ ​ FID = FID protected − FID clean \Delta\mathrm{FID}=\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{protected}}-\mathrm{FID}_{\mathrm{clean}} [ 28 ] ; values near or below zero indicate no measured quality loss, whereas large positive values indicate degradation. Unless stated otherwise, SpectralCanary uses α = 0.02 \alpha=0.02 , c = 0.20 c=0.20 , and δ = 1 \delta=1 . Every model-training and image-sampling setting is repeated with three independent runs. Detailed protocols are in Appx. A .

sections.heading: 4.2 Per-Generation Discrimination Survives Changes to Models and Training Data

sections.heading: 4.3 The Same Setting Works Across Five Image Types
sections.text: Figure 4 : SpectralCanary works consistently across five image types. Each point shows one method on one dataset. The vertical axis is the per-generation TPR at 1 % 1\% FPR: the percentage of outputs from protected-data models detected while 1 % 1\% of outputs from clean-data models are falsely flagged. In (a), the horizontal axis measures the change in the trained model’s output quality; zero means no change. In (b), it measures the change from an original image to its protected copy; zero means identical images. The best results are near the upper-left corner. We next test whether the same SpectralCanary setting works beyond Pokemon by asking three questions: Does a single generated output support reliable per-generation discrimination? Do the protected images still resemble the originals? Does training on those images degrade model outputs? SpectralCanary performs well on all three questions. At a per-generation FPR of 1 % 1\% , it achieves an average per-generation TPR of 92.4 % 92.4\% across outputs from models trained on protected data. The protected images remain close to their originals: average LPIPS is 0.022 0.022 , where zero means identical images. Training on the protected images causes almost no average change in model output quality: mean Δ \Delta FID is 0.05 0.05 , where zero means no change. On the sparse Sketch-Scene drawings, SpectralCanary achieves 100 % 100\% per-generation TPR with LPIPS 0.002 0.002 . The hardest dataset is RSICD, where it achieves 78.9 % 78.9\% per-generation TPR with LPIPS 0.048 0.048 . Fig. 4 compares all methods. Each point shows one method on one dataset. Good results appear near the upper-left corner: high per-generation TPR with little change to either the training images or the trained model’s outputs. sections.heading: 4.4 Protection Is Fast as Well as Effective
sections.text: Figure 5 : SpectralCanary achieves high per-generation discrimination with low quality and runtime cost. Average per-generation TPR at 1 % 1\% FPR over the eight Pokemon settings is compared with (a) change in FID, (b) protection time, and (c) paired-image LPIPS. Preferred results lie upward and to the left. EnTruth adds 0.5 % 0.5\% auxiliary samples, so paired-image LPIPS is not defined for it. SpectralCanary protects an image in 0.39 0.39 seconds on CPU while retaining the highest average per-generation TPR. Fig. 5 compares per-generation discrimination with generated-image quality, protection time, and image distortion on Pokemon. DIAGNOSIS is faster, but its average TPR is only 32.2 % 32.2\% . SIREN and EnTruth require substantially more computation while achieving lower per-generation TPR. SpectralCanary also has no average FID penalty and the lowest paired-image LPIPS among the methods that modify every image. These timings are hardware-dependent, and CPU and GPU measurements are not perfectly interchangeable; their main purpose is to distinguish a single deterministic FFT-based transform from methods that require generating auxiliary images or performing iterative optimization. Appx. E gives the complete timing results.

sections.heading: 4.5 Low Frequencies Carry the Trace More Reliably
sections.text: Figure 6 : Matched low-frequency traces transfer more reliably than mid- or high-frequency traces. Points show mean per-generation TPR at 1 % 1\% FPR over three canary images. Arrows show the performance gaps. The advantage of low frequencies remains after controlling for the amount of spectral change. We compare disjoint low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands on Pokemon and ROCOv2 with SD1.5. The bands contain the same number of Fourier coefficients, and we give them the same total amount of Fourier-domain change as the deployed smooth low-pass mask. This comparison prevents one band from winning merely because it changes more of the image. Fig. 6 shows that the low-frequency band has the highest per-generation TPR on both datasets. It exceeds the high-frequency band by 16.9 16.9 percentage points on Pokemon and 88.9 88.9 points on ROCOv2; the mid-frequency band is also weaker in both cases. Appx. K describes the construction, and Tab. 6 reports per-generation discrimination, image fidelity, generated-image quality, and variation across three canary images.

sections.heading: 4.6 Removal Attacks Damage Quality Before Erasing the Trace
sections.text: Figure 7 : The evaluated attacks erase the trace only after causing substantial damage. From the unattacked point, stronger attacks move down and to the right, indicating per-generation TPR falls, but Δ \Delta FID and LPIPS increase. The clean-training marker shows the target TPR. In our evaluated attacks, substantially reducing per-generation TPR also substantially damages the training data or the resulting model. The attacker knows the protection algorithm and may know α \alpha and c c , but not the canary, original images, or verifier. We test three attacks. A donor is an unrelated, unprotected image whose low-frequency content is used as a replacement source. Fixed-donor replacement uses the same donor for all protected images. Per-image replacement uses a different donor for each image. The third attack estimates the shared low-frequency pattern directly from the protected collection and removes it. Appx. M gives the equations and settings. Fig. 7 follows each attack from mild to aggressive removal. Mild attacks leave per-generation TPR largely intact. Driving TPR toward the clean-training baseline requires more than 25 additional FID points under the strongest evaluated attack and also produces large LPIPS changes. This establishes a removal–quality boundary for these three attacks; it is not a guarantee against every possible attack, especially one that can inspect the model or verifier.

sections.heading: 5 Limitations and Responsible Use
sections.text: Our evaluation covers two T2I architecture families, five datasets, and both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning. It does not establish transfer to every model, or mixture of a protected collection with a larger unprotected corpus. The main experiments also use one fixed natural canary image. Although the phase-randomized controls in Appx. L isolate the role of spatial coherence, broader evaluation across independently chosen canary images and key reuse is needed. The adaptive evaluation assumes that the canary image and verifier remain private. If the attacker learns V V , α \alpha , and c c , Eq. 6 permits exact inversion before clipping or quantization. The three evaluated attacks (fixed-donor replacement, per-image donor replacement, and shared-structure estimation) characterize only this secrecy-dependent threat model and do not provide a cryptographic or white-box robustness guarantee. Future evaluations should consider collusion across releases, learned removal models, stronger shared-structure estimators, and adaptive access to verifier feedback. SSIM, LPIPS, and FID capture only part of image fidelity and generative utility. Human perceptual studies and task-specific utility measurements would be needed to support stronger claims about invisibility or harmlessness. Likewise, our KS-test rejection rates on protected-data models estimate statistical power under the stated sampling protocol, while fixed-threshold model-level verification uses separate clean-data and protected-data models for calibration. A deployment would require broader calibration across representative clean-data models and should treat a positive result as statistical evidence under the threat model, not as standalone proof of unauthorized use. SpectralCanary is intended to help data owners audit model customization, but proactive traces can also be inserted into data without the knowledge of downstream users. Responsible use requires authorization to modify the collection, disclosure where appropriate, respect for dataset licenses, and safeguards against unsupported attribution. Decisions with legal or reputational consequences should combine the audit with independent evidence.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose SpectralCanary, a deterministic and inexpensive approach to proactive T2I dataset-use auditing. SpectralCanary injects a weak shared visual trace through a smooth low-pass mask while leaving captions unchanged. Across eight Pokemon model–transformation settings, it provides the strongest average per-generation discrimination and reliable KS-based multi-query auditing among the evaluated methods. The same operating point generalizes across five visual domains while preserving protected-image fidelity and generative utility. Matched-energy frequency-location experiments further show that low-frequency placement transfers more consistently than mid/high-frequency placement across datasets. Finally, the adaptive evaluation identifies a scoped robustness boundary, showing that the evaluated sanitization attacks substantially reduce per-generation TPR only at the cost of considerable image-quality or generative-utility degradation. Together, these results establish SpectralCanary as a practical method for T2I dataset-use auditing, while the limitations discussed above motivate future work.

sections.heading: Fine-tuning and auditing across methods.
sections.text: We follow Li et al. [13] for the main setting and use at most 1,000 1{,}000 training images. For each dataset, backbone, method, and transformation, we train one clean-data and one protected-data LoRA. SD1.5 uses resolution 512 × 512 512\times 512 , batch size 4 4 , LoRA rank 64 64 , AdamW, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and 80 80 epochs. Generation uses Euler ancestral sampling with 30 30 steps and classifier-free guidance 7.5 7.5 . SD3.5 uses LoRA rank 16 16 , learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , AdamW, a constant schedule, and 80 80 epochs. Its objective uses the unpreconditioned linear flow-matching target u = ϵ − x 0 u=\epsilon-x_{0} . SD3.5 generations use resolution 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 and 30 30 steps. The clean-data and protected-data models receive the same ordered prompt list, and every generation is scored independently. SIREN and SpectralCanary use original captions as audit prompts; DIAGNOSIS appends its trigger token; EnTruth uses method-specific trigger prompts. SD1.5 experiments generate 1,000 1{,}000 images per model and SD3.5 experiments generate 500 500 .

sections.heading: EnTruth [ 25 ] .
sections.text: As there is no official code, we follow its shared-template pipeline. Candidate templates use the prompts “billboard for big sale”, “a painting with a frame”, “photo frame with a family”, “a window with mountains outside”. Foregrounds use “fruits for sale” and “fruit stand”, with 50 50 images per foreground prompt and one per template prompt, generated by SD1.5. The hard trigger is “[Tgr]”, the soft trigger keyword is “fruit”. The injected samples rate is 0.5 % 0.5\% . An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 verifier uses selected templated samples as positives and original samples as negatives. The main paper reports the stronger hard-trigger result from Appx. P .

sections.heading: DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] .
sections.text: We follow the official code. DIAGNOSIS applies a WaNet-style image transformation [ 18 ] to 20 % 20\% of the training set, uses hard trigger token “ tq ”, and sets k = 128 k=128 and s = 1.0 s=1.0 . An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 classifier uses transformed images as positives and their originals as negatives.

sections.heading: SIREN [ 13 ] .
sections.text: We follow the official code. SIREN first trains a clean-data LoRA initialization, then fine-tunes its encoder–decoder for 60 60 epochs. The learned encoder–decoder protects the full dataset and directly scores generated samples. No trigger prompt is required.

sections.heading: SpectralCanary protection and export.
sections.text: We use the fixed RGB canary in Fig. 1 (b). Protection is applied at the stored image resolution before downstream resizing or transformations. We convert to sRGB, scale channels to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , resize the canary with antialiased bicubic interpolation, apply the unitary channel-wise transform, discard numerical imaginary residue, clip to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , quantize to 8-bit RGB, and save lossless PNG files. Defaults are δ = 1 \delta=1 , α = 0.02 \alpha=0.02 , and c = 0.20 c=0.20 . For δ < 1 \delta<1 , the run seed selects subset ℐ δ \mathcal{I}_{\delta} for both protection and verifier training.

sections.heading: SpectralCanary verifier.
sections.text: We initialize an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 [ 9 ] with a binary head. Source indices are split 80 / 20 80/20 before pairing, so each original and protected counterpart stays in the same partition. Inputs are resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 and ImageNet-normalized without stochastic augmentation. We fine-tune all layers with AdamW, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , batch size 32 32 , and 20 20 epochs, selecting the lowest validation-loss checkpoint. Each dataset and run trains a separate verifier without T2I generations.

sections.heading: Data transformations.
sections.text: • Training-time augmentation. Images first pass through the bucketed training resize and are randomly cropped when larger than the target resolution. With probability 0.33 0.33 , color augmentation applies either a hue shift in [ − 8 , 8 ] [-8,8] degrees or gamma adjustment with γ ∼ U ⁡ ( 0.95 , 1.05 ) \gamma\sim U(0.95,1.05) . Horizontal flipping has probability 0.5 0.5 . • Prompt recaptioning. Every caption is rewritten using Qwen2.5-VL 7B Instruct; images remain unchanged. The prompt is: Rewrite the caption for this image as a high-quality caption. Keep the important visual content, remove redundant wording, and avoid mentioning text quality, watermarks, camera metadata, or that this is a rewrite. Output only the rewritten caption. Current caption: {current_caption} • Image regeneration. WatermarkAttacker uses the sd2-community Stable Diffusion 2.1 checkpoint, VAE encoding, noise_step=60 , 50 50 denoising steps, guidance 7.5 7.5 , an empty prompt, and fixed seed 1024 1024 . It preserves the source resolution. The regenerated datasets train suspect LoRAs under the same downstream protocol.

evaluation measures how well verifier scores separate generations from clean-data and protected-data models. This protocol enables a controlled comparison across methods without threshold calibration or query aggregation. Fixed-threshold model-level verification instead translates aggregated per-generation scores into a model-level decision that answers: was a suspect model trained on the protected dataset? We first calibrate a model-level decision threshold and then keep it fixed for all held-out evaluations. For each method and T2I architecture, we reserve one independently trained clean-data model 𝒢 cal − \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cal}}^{-} and one protected-data model 𝒢 cal + \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cal}}^{+} for threshold calibration. Given K K audit prompts, we generate one image per prompt and define the aggregate score of a model 𝒢 \mathcal{G} as q K ​ ( 𝒢 ) = 1 K ​ ∑ j = 1 K f θ ​ ( y j 𝒢 ) , q_{K}(\mathcal{G})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}f_{\theta}\!\left(y_{j}^{\mathcal{G}}\right), (12) where f θ f_{\theta} is the method-specific verifier and y j 𝒢 y_{j}^{\mathcal{G}} is the image generated for prompt j j . For calibration, we use all available generations with K cal = 1000 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=1000 for SD1.5 and K cal = 500 K_{\mathrm{cal}}=500 for SD3.5. We set the method–architecture-specific threshold to the midpoint between the clean-data and protected-data calibration scores: t = q K cal ​ ( 𝒢 cal − ) + q K cal ​ ( 𝒢 cal + ) 2 . t=\frac{q_{K_{\mathrm{cal}}}(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cal}}^{-})+q_{K_{\mathrm{cal}}}(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cal}}^{+})}{2}. (13) The midpoint provides a simple symmetric decision boundary between the two calibration models without favoring either class. The calibration models are excluded from evaluation. Each threshold is calibrated once under the no-transformation setting and then held fixed across all transformation settings, so evaluation does not assume prior knowledge of the transformation applied by the unauthorized trainer. For each method, architecture, and transformation setting, we independently train five clean-data and five protected-data test models using different random seeds. Each suspect model is evaluated using only K test = 30 K_{\mathrm{test}}=30 queries and is classified as trained on protected data when q 30 ​ ( 𝒢 ) ≥ t . q_{30}(\mathcal{G})\geq t. Across 4 methods, 2 architectures, and 4 transformation settings, this gives 320 held-out test models. We report TPR, FPR, precision, F1 score, and accuracy over the resulting model-level decisions. To quantify variation due to the 30-query budget, we repeat the query subsampling 1,000 times from the available held-out generations and report the mean and standard deviation across these resampled query sets.

Reactive methods leave the released data unchanged and later test whether a model was trained on it. Membership inference estimates whether a particular image or prompt–image pair belonged to the training set; recent work studies this problem for fine-tuned diffusion models in black-box settings [ 3 , 21 , 44 , 45 ] . RECOVER [ 35 ] instead identifies individual fine-tuning images through their increased robustness under stochastic inversion–reconstruction, without modifying the images or requiring the pre-fine-tuned model. Other methods compare generated images with protected examples using representations such as CLIP [ 23 ] or DINO [ 19 ] . These methods apply to collections that have already been published, but their evidence can weaken when a T2I model generalizes without retaining identifiable information about individual samples [ 13 , 25 , 14 ] . Proactive protection and auditing. Anti-learning methods, including Glaze [ 30 ] , AdvDM [ 43 ] , Anti-DreamBooth [ 32 ] , FastProtect [ 1 ] , and MetaCloak [ 15 ] , modify images to prevent or redirect unauthorized customization. Proactive dataset-use auditing instead inserts a signal intended to transfer into the customized model. Its goal is not to make fine-tuning fail, but to make outputs from a model trained on the protected collection statistically distinguishable from outputs of clean-data reference models. Pixel-level traces. DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] , DiffusionShield [ 6 ] , FT-Shield [ 5 ] , and SIREN [ 13 ] insert watermarks, transformations, or trigger-like signals that can later be detected in generated images. Their protected images remain close to the originals, but weak nonsemantic signals may be attenuated by image editing, regeneration, augmentation, or a change in T2I backbone. SpectralCanary shares the goal of preserving image appearance but uses a common low-frequency visual component rather than an optimized or pixel-local signal. Explicit visual canaries. EnTruth [ 25 ] inserts samples with a repeated visual template and a textual trigger. The coherent template transfers more readily than a weak pixel-level pattern, but the samples are visibly out of distribution (Appx. O ) and can be removed by visual filtering or caption cleaning. SpectralCanary instead distributes a weak version of the same visual component across the original collection and does not alter captions. Relation to T2I data poisoning. Dataset-use auditing and data poisoning both modify training data so that the resulting model acquires an additional behavior [ 29 , 8 , 36 , 10 ] . BBadT2I [ 40 ] implants trigger-dependent pixel-, object-, or style-level behaviors. Nightshade [ 31 ] corrupts targeted concepts through modified image–text pairs, Bilateral Data Poisoning [ 20 ] induces persistent backdoor behavior, and SilentBadDiffusion [ 33 ] elicits attacker-specified content under trigger prompts. Silent Branding [ 12 ] is especially relevant because it modifies only images and induces reproduction of a repeated visual logo without a textual trigger. We adapt it as a dataset-use auditing baseline under the same downstream fine-tuning and auditing protocol (Appx. Q ).

Proactive dataset-use auditing plants a shared signal in a dataset before release, then later checks whether that signal appears in a suspect model’s generated outputs. Existing approaches often trade off verifiability, fidelity, robustness, and deployability. We introduce SpectralCanary , which uses a smooth low-pass mask to blend a fixed canary image into every collection image while leaving captions unchanged and requiring neither auxiliary generation nor per-image optimization. A lightweight verifier detects the transferred signal in suspect-model outputs. Across eight tests on the Pokemon dataset and three realistic data transformations, spanning two architectures families, SpectralCanary achieves the highest average per-generation TPR@ 1 % 1\% FPR ( 91.1 % 91.1\% ) and fixed threshold model-level accuracy using 30 generations ( 94.8 % 94.8\% ) among the evaluated methods. Across five datasets spanning artistic, medical, satellite, and fashion domains with SD3.5, SpectralCanary averages 92.4 % 92.4\% per-generation TPR@ 1 % 1\% FPR while preserving the released images (SSIM 0.989 0.989 , LPIPS 0.022 0.022 ) with a near-zero mean change FID (mean Δ \Delta FID 0.05 0.05 ) across datasets. Matched-energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2 support our design choice, low-frequency placement transfers more reliably compared to mid/high-frequency placement. Under the evaluated adaptive attacks, the most effective removal requires aggressive modification and incurs more than 25 25 Δ \Delta FID points. These results identify low-frequency visual signals as effective carriers for collection-level T2I audit traces. SpectralCanary: Embarrassingly Simple Low-Frequency Traces for T2I Dataset-Use Auditing Sy-Tuyen Ho \affmark 1 Anirudh Satheesh Soham Chawathe \affmark 1 Huy Nghiem \affmark 1 \apauthor Yongkyun Lee \apauthor Andrew Adams Schoen \apauthor [1]Furong Huang keywords Dataset-Use Auditing, Text to Image, Data Provenance 1 Introduction Creative and scientific image collections embody substantial human labor, expertise, and investment. Adapting text-to-image (T2I) models to such collections can support legitimate personalization, education, design, and scientific communication [ 26 , 7 , 11 ] . The same capability, however, allows a third party to fine-tune and deploy a model on a collection without the rights holder’s consent, attribution, or compensation. Because a model can absorb a collection’s visual characteristics without reproducing individual images, rights holders may have little evidence that their work was used [ 21 , 13 ] . Practical dataset-use auditing can strengthen accountability and licensing compliance while allowing images to remain available for legitimate use. Figure 1 : SpectralCanary overview. (a) Auditing workflow. An owner protects a collection before release, then queries a suspect T2I model and tests whether its generated outputs contain the canary. (b) Spectral hybridization. SpectralCanary blends a fixed canary through a smooth low-pass mask M c M_{c} with strength α \alpha , retaining most of the remaining spectrum. A lightweight verifier trained on original–protected pairs detects the trace in model generations. (c) Visual fidelity. Original–protected pairs across five datasets, including sparse sketches. We study proactive dataset-use auditing, commonly termed data traceability or unauthorized data-use verification in prior works. A practical method should satisfy four requirements. (Req. 1) Collection-level verifiability. It should provide evidence from black-box outputs even when no training image is reproduced. (Req. 2) Fidelity and utility preservation. Protected samples should preserve their original appearance and the utility of models trained on them, avoiding harm to legitimate use while resisting easy filtering. (Req. 3) Pipeline robustness. The trace should remain detectable across model architectures, after augmentation such as image regeneration or recaptioning. (Req. 4) Operational deployability. The protection transform should be model-agnostic and scale efficiently to large collections without auxiliary generation or iterative per-image optimization. Prior approaches typically sacrifice at least one requirement. Reactive auditing: limited collection-level evidence (Req. 1). Membership and similarity tests rely on sample-specific evidence that generalization may erase [ 21 , 13 ] . Pixel-level watermarks: limited robustness (Req. 3). Weak signals may be attenuated by augmentation, regeneration, or fail to transfer across model backbones [ 34 , 13 ] . Explicit canaries: fidelity and robustness trade-offs (Reqs. 2–3). Repeated templates can be conspicuous and filterable, while recaptioning can remove textual triggers [ 25 ] . Adjacent data-poisoning objectives. Poisoning induces chosen behavior rather than provides evidence of dataset use. Persistent behavior may not be unique or reliably elicited, so it does not by itself establish use of a particular collection [ 33 , 12 ] . Across proactive methods, auxiliary generation, filtering, and iterative optimization can also limit deployability (Req. 4) by increasing computational cost or requiring external models, domain-specific assumptions [ 25 , 13 , 12 ] . These limitations motivate a subtle, transferable, caption-independent, and inexpensive trace. We propose SpectralCanary , whose key design choice is the frequency band used for the shared trace. Before release, the dataset owner chooses one fixed canary image. For each collection image, SpectralCanary mixes a small amount of the canary’s low-frequency Fourier content into the original while retaining most of its spectrum and leaving its caption unchanged (Fig. 1 (b)). The protected spectra are thereby shifted toward a common low-frequency target, creating a collection-level signal. Low frequencies encode broad spatial structure that neural networks preferentially learn [ 24 , 37 ] and that is important to T2I generation [ 39 , 17 ] . This motivates our hypothesis that a weak low-frequency trace can transfer during fine-tuning. The dataset owner then queries a suspect model and uses a lightweight verifier to test whether its generated outputs contain the trace (Fig. 1 (a)). Importantly, SpectralCanary uses a single deterministic transform requiring no caption changes, auxiliary generator, or per-image optimization. We evaluate all four requirements. Robustness tests cover a convolutional latent-diffusion U-Net [ 26 ] , a transformer-based rectified-flow model [ 7 ] ; data augmentation, image regeneration [ 42 ] , and recaptioning. Direct baselines include pixel-level traces (SIREN [ 13 ] , DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] ) and explicit canaries (EnTruth [ 25 ] ). We also adapt Silent Branding [ 12 ] but report its evaluation separately in Appx. Q , because it targets visual branding rather than dataset-use auditing. Auditing effectiveness and robustness. For per-generation discrimination, AUC measures verifier-score separation, while TPR at 1% FPR measures detection of outputs from protected-data models. Across eight Pokemon settings, SpectralCanary achieves 98.0% AUC and 91.1% TPR. In fixed-threshold model-level verification using 30 generations, it achieves 94.8% average accuracy under the same settings. Fidelity and utility preservation. SSIM and LPIPS compare original and protected images, while Δ \Delta FID measures the change in generative quality. Across five visual domains with SD3.5, SpectralCanary achieves 99.5 % 99.5\% AUC and 92.4 % 92.4\% TPR with SSIM 0.989 0.989 , LPIPS 0.022 0.022 , with a near-zero mean change FID ( Δ \Delta FID 0.05 0.05 ). On sparse Sketch-Scene drawings, it achieves 100 % 100\% AUC and TPR with SSIM 0.997 0.997 and LPIPS 0.002 0.002 . Operational deployability. Protection takes 0.39 0.39 seconds per image on our CPU setup (Appx. E ). Mechanism and boundary. In matched-energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2, we show that low-frequency placement transfers more reliably compared to mid/high-frequency placement. Within the evaluated adaptive attacks, effective removal requires aggressive modification and incurs more than 25 25 Δ \Delta FID points. Our main contributions are: • We identify low-frequency visual structure as an effective carrier for weak collection-level traces during T2I fine-tuning. In matched band size and perturbation energy ablations on Pokemon and ROCOv2 with SD1.5, we show that low-frequency placement yields higher per-generation TPR than mid/high-frequency placement. • We introduce SpectralCanary, a deterministic and caption-preserving spectral hybridization method. Reactive methods test an already trained model using membership inference or similarity between generated and reference images [ 3 , 21 , 23 , 19 ] . Such evidence can weaken when fine-tuning transfers collection-level characteristics without retaining identifiable information about individual samples. Proactive methods instead modify a collection before release. Anti-learning methods aim to prevent or redirect customization [ 30 , 43 , 32 , 1 , 15 ] . Proactive traceability aims to preserve customization utility while making later use statistically auditable. Proactive traceability. Pixel-level methods such as DIAGNOSIS [ 34 ] and SIREN [ 13 ] insert weak transformations or learned signals that can be detected in generated images. Their subtle signals preserve appearance, but can be attenuated by augmentation, regeneration, or model backbone changes. EnTruth instead inserts explicit canary samples containing a repeated template and textual trigger [ 25 ] . This coherent signal can transfer strongly, but the injected samples are conspicuous and caption triggers can be removed. Our direct comparisons span the two main proactive families including subtle pixel-level traces and explicit visual canary samples. Relation to poisoning. Data poisoning induces chosen behaviors such as concept corruption, reproduction, or persistent branding [ 33 , 12 ] . Persistence alone is insufficient for auditing. Auditing instead requires a collection-specific signal detectable under ordinary, trigger-free queries with controlled false positives. SpectralCanary targets this auditing objective rather than model corruption. Appx. It does not establish transfer to every model, or mixture of a protected collection with a larger unprotected corpus. The main experiments also use one fixed natural canary image. Although the phase-randomized controls in Appx. L isolate the role of spatial coherence, broader evaluation across independently chosen canary images and key reuse is needed. The adaptive evaluation assumes that the canary image and verifier remain private. If the attacker learns V V , α \alpha , and c c , Eq. 6 permits exact inversion before clipping or quantization. The three evaluated attacks (fixed-donor replacement, per-image donor replacement, and shared-structure estimation) characterize only this secrecy-dependent threat model and do not provide a cryptographic or white-box robustness guarantee. Future evaluations should consider collusion across releases, learned removal models, stronger shared-structure estimators, and adaptive access to verifier feedback. SSIM, LPIPS, and FID capture only part of image fidelity and generative utility. Human perceptual studies and task-specific utility measurements would be needed to support stronger claims about invisibility or harmlessness. Likewise, our KS-test rejection rates on protected-data models estimate statistical power under the stated sampling protocol, while fixed-threshold model-level verification uses separate clean-data and protected-data models for calibration. A deployment would require broader calibration across representative clean-data models and should treat a positive result as statistical evidence under the threat model, not as standalone proof of unauthorized use. SpectralCanary is intended to help data owners audit model customization, but proactive traces can also be inserted into data without the knowledge of downstream users. Responsible use requires authorization to modify the collection, disclosure where appropriate, respect for dataset licenses, and safeguards against unsupported attribution. Decisions with legal or reputational consequences should combine the audit with independent evidence. 6 Conclusion We propose SpectralCanary, a deterministic and inexpensive approach to proactive T2I dataset-use auditing. SpectralCanary injects a weak shared visual trace through a smooth low-pass mask while leaving captions unchanged. Across eight Pokemon model–transformation settings, it provides the strongest average per-generation discrimination and reliable KS-based multi-query auditing among the evaluated methods. The same operating point generalizes across five visual domains while preserving protected-image fidelity and generative utility. Matched-energy frequency-location experiments further show that low-frequency placement transfers more consistently than mid/high-frequency placement across datasets. Finally, the adaptive evaluation identifies a scoped robustness boundary, showing that the evaluated sanitization attacks substantially reduce per-generation TPR only at the cost of considerable image-quality or generative-utility degradation. Together, these results establish SpectralCanary as a practical method for T2I dataset-use auditing, while the limitations discussed above motivate future work.
